questions.explain: RDS for SQL Server has no in-engine ML invocation and no ML Services, so the production pattern is to score outside the engine with a scheduled Lambda, land predictions in a table like dbo.churn_predictions, and JOIN it in T-SQL.
options: Call the SageMaker endpoint synchronously from a T-SQL trigger on the write path
Pre-compute predictions with a scheduled Lambda/SageMaker job into a dedicated predictions table that T-SQL JOINs against
Install SQL Server Machine Learning Services on the RDS instance and call sp_execute_external_script per row
Use SQLCLR to invoke Bedrock directly from within stored procedures
questions.q: What is the production pattern for ML inference on RDS for SQL Server, which offers no in-engine ML invocation?

questions.explain: The chapter warns that inference calls add 50–200ms latency under normal conditions — fine for an async scheduled scoring batch, but not on a sub-10ms OLTP write path, so scoring must stay asynchronous.
options: SageMaker endpoints cannot be invoked from a Lambda function
SageMaker only supports batch transforms, not real-time endpoints
Lambda functions are billed per invocation and would double the AWS bill
Inference API calls add 50–200ms of latency, which is unacceptable on an OLTP write path that needs sub-10ms response times
questions.q: Why is calling a SageMaker or Comprehend endpoint synchronously from the application write path an anti-pattern?

questions.explain: Performance Insights ML builds a per-metric baseline from about two weeks of historical data and flags deviations using a threshold derived from that baseline — a learned threshold, not a static one the DBA configures.
options: It builds a baseline model from roughly two weeks of historical data and derives a learned threshold from that baseline
It uses static thresholds configured by the DBA per wait event in the RDS console
It compares current DB load against the provisioned vCPU count of the instance class
It fires an alert whenever any wait event exceeds 5 vCPUs of DB load
questions.q: How does Performance Insights ML derive the threshold it uses to flag anomalous wait events?

questions.explain: The chapter frames the gap explicitly: PI ML tells you *what* is anomalous, while DevOps Guru (ML trained on fleet operational data) attempts to tell you *why* and what to do — root cause hypotheses called insights.
options: Performance Insights ML works on Aurora only; DevOps Guru works on RDS for SQL Server
Performance Insights ML generates DDL recommendations; DevOps Guru applies them automatically
DevOps Guru is a replacement for Performance Insights and CloudWatch Logs
Performance Insights ML tells you what metric is anomalous; DevOps Guru correlates anomalies with logs and events to tell you why and what to do
questions.q: What is the key distinction between Performance Insights ML and DevOps Guru for RDS?

questions.explain: The chapter's rules: REBUILD at >= 30% fragmentation and page_count > 5000, REORGANIZE at 5–30%, skip indexes under 1000 pages (rebuilding them wastes log space), and UPDATE STATISTICS where stats_age_days > 7 — all online with WITH (ONLINE = ON).
options: REBUILD for fragmentation >= 30% and page_count > 5000; REORGANIZE for 5–30%; skip indexes under 1000 pages; UPDATE STATISTICS where stats are older than 7 days
REBUILD for fragmentation >= 10%; REORGANIZE for anything under 10%; always use SORT_IN_TEMPDB
REORGANIZE for fragmentation >= 30%; REBUILD for 5–30%; rebuild everything weekly regardless of size
REBUILD all indexes monthly with MAXDOP = 0; statistics update automatically so no explicit UPDATE STATISTICS needed
